summaries.example: Imagine you learn from a weather app that it is very cold outside. You use that fact to figure out that you have never been outside in colder weather. Your reason for the first idea helps support the second idea. But sometimes a reason cannot pass along its support. For example, if you can trust that someone is Jessica only because you already know she is not her identical twin Jocelyn, then the first idea cannot be used to newly support the second one.
summaries.summary: The entry studies how reasons for believing one statement can support another statement through reasoning. This is called transmission of justification. For example, evidence that a person has a dangerous illness may support the prediction that the person will soon die, if the connection is understood. But support does not always travel from a premise, the starting idea, to a conclusion. Sometimes the evidence supports the premise only because the person already has independent support for the conclusion. Then the argument is circular in an important way, and it cannot give the conclusion new support. The entry also distinguishes transmission from closure: closure says that a person has support for the conclusion, while transmission asks whether that support comes from the premise and the known link. Philosophers use these ideas to study difficult arguments about perception, the outside world, and knowledge.
key_ideas: People often use evidence for one belief to support another belief that follows from it.
Transmission needs both a supported starting idea and an understanding of how the conclusion follows.
Support can fail to pass along when the starting evidence already depends on the conclusion.
An argument may support its conclusion in another way without transmitting support from its premise.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use reasoning every day in school, science, and ordinary decisions. Understanding transmission helps us ask whether a conclusion is really supported by the reason given, or whether the conclusion was quietly assumed from the start. It also helps explain why some clever-looking arguments do not convince someone who does not already accept their main assumption.

important_terms.definition: A reason or piece of evidence that makes it sensible to believe something.
When support for one idea helps support another idea that follows from it.
A statement or idea that follows logically from another statement or idea.
A situation where an argument cannot pass its support to its conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Can a reason for one idea always support every idea that follows from it?
Why might needing the conclusion first make an argument circular?
What is the difference between having support for an idea and getting new support through an argument?

summaries.example: Suppose you see animals in a zoo enclosure that look exactly like zebras. You infer that they are zebras, and then infer that they are not mules painted to look like zebras. The second inference is logically valid if the first claim is true. Yet some philosophers argue that the visual evidence may support the first claim only if you already have independent reason to rule out the disguised-mule possibility. If so, the evidence does not transmit its support to the conclusion, even though the entailment is understood.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a central issue in epistemology: when does justification for a premise transmit to a conclusion? The basic case involves a subject who has justification for p from evidence e, knows that p entails q, and thereby obtains justification for q in virtue of the first two facts. This final “in virtue of” condition separates transmission from epistemic closure. Closure merely says that justification extends to q; transmission explains the source of that justification. The entry also allows that transmission may give first-time justification, an independent additional reason, or a strengthening of an already existing reason. Transmission failure can be trivial, as when the premise is not justified or the entailment is not known. The more important cases are non-transmissive arguments, where the argument would not transmit the relevant support even if those conditions were satisfied. Proposed explanations include premise-circularity, dependence on collateral information, and indirectness, in which the evidence supports the conclusion directly. Other accounts analyze reliability or argue that certain reasoning procedures defeat themselves. These distinctions are used in debates about perception, skeptical hypotheses, Moore’s proof of an external world, religiously based arguments, and McKinsey’s paradox.
key_ideas: A standard account analyzes transmission using three elements: justification for p from evidence, knowledge that p entails q, and justification for q in virtue of those two elements.
Transmission is stronger than closure. Closure concerns whether q is justified; transmission concerns why q is justified.
Transmission can provide first-time justification, independent additional justification, or support that strengthens an existing degree of justification.
Some failures are trivial because a premise is not justified or the entailment is not known. More interesting failures occur even when those conditions are met.
Premise-circularity, information-dependence, and indirectness are major proposed sources of non-transmissivity.
The entry applies the debate to Moorean arguments about the external world and to McKinsey’s paradox about self-knowledge and externalism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic shows why logical validity is not the whole story about good reasoning. An argument can have a valid form while failing to give its conclusion the kind of support its premise possesses. This matters when evaluating scientific inferences, responses to skepticism, claims about perception, and arguments that attempt to derive empirical knowledge from apparently non-empirical premises. It also clarifies disagreements: some philosophers say an argument transmits justification but is ineffective for persuading a doubter, while others say the argument itself is non-transmissive.

important_terms.definition: Epistemic support for believing a proposition; in the entry, the focus is mainly on propositional justification.
The passing of justification for a premise to a conclusion because the subject understands that the conclusion follows from the premise.
The idea that if someone is justified in believing a premise and knows that it entails a conclusion, they are justified in believing the conclusion.
A proposition that follows necessarily from another proposition or set of propositions.
An argument that cannot transmit justification based on specified evidence, under any relevant epistemic circumstances.
A pattern in which evidence supports a premise only given background information that itself requires independent support for the conclusion.
A case where evidence directly supports the conclusion, making the inference through the premise an unnecessary detour.
Additional support that increases the strength of an already justified conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Can a conclusion be justified without being justified through the argument that led someone to it?
Does a deductively valid argument automatically transmit justification? Why might philosophers distinguish validity from transmission?
If evidence supports both a premise and its conclusion directly, is the inference doing epistemic work?
Should an argument count as successful if it gives support only to someone who already accepts its conclusion?
How might failures of transmission affect arguments against skepticism?

summaries.example: A student sees a classmate wearing a team jersey and reasons: “That looks like Maya, so it is Maya; if it is Maya, then it is not her identical twin, Naya.” The first step may seem reasonable. But if the student can identify someone as Maya only because the student already knows the person is not Naya, then the evidence cannot give the second claim fresh support. The reasoning depends on the conclusion it was supposed to establish.
summaries.summary: This entry asks how epistemic support moves through reasoning. If a person has justification for a premise p from evidence e, understands that p entails q, and gains justification for q because of those facts, justification has transmitted from p to q. This is common in deduction: a justified hypothesis can support a prediction that follows from it. However, transmission is not identical to closure. Closure says that justification for p and knowledge of the entailment result in justification for q; transmission adds the requirement that the support for q comes from the premise’s support and the inference itself. The entry discusses several kinds of transmission. A person may gain first-time justification for q, an additional independent reason for q, or stronger justification for q than they had before. Failure can be trivial when a required condition is missing. More significant cases involve non-transmissive arguments: even when the premise is justified and the entailment is known, the argument cannot pass along the relevant support. One explanation is information-dependence, where the evidence supports p only because background information already supports q. Another is indirectness, where the evidence supports q directly, so reasoning through p adds no support. These ideas are applied to arguments about perception, skeptical possibilities, Moore’s proof, religious justification, and McKinsey’s paradox.
key_ideas: In ordinary reasoning, evidence for a premise often supports a conclusion that follows from it.
Transmission requires more than a valid argument: the conclusion must be supported because of the justified premise and the understood entailment.
Closure and transmission can come apart. A person may be justified in believing the conclusion, but not because the argument transmitted support to it.
Some transmission failures are uninteresting: the person lacks justification for the premise or does not recognize the logical link.
A deeper problem occurs when evidence supports the premise only with help from independent support for the conclusion.
Philosophers disagree about whether examples involving perception and skepticism fail to transmit or merely fail to persuade certain audiences.
summaries.why_it_matters: Good reasoning is not just a matter of reaching a true conclusion or using a valid pattern. We also need to know whether the reasons actually support the conclusion in the required way. The distinction is useful for checking arguments in science, school discussions, and philosophy. It explains why an argument may look convincing to one person but fail to give new support to someone who doubts its starting assumptions. It also gives philosophers a precise way to compare competing explanations of skepticism and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: Good evidence or a good reason for holding a belief.
The process by which support for one claim carries over to a claim that follows from it.
A claim that must be true if another claim is true.
A rule saying that justification for a claim plus knowledge of what it entails gives justification for the consequence.
A failure in which the conclusion does not receive support because of the premise and the known logical connection.
Reasoning that depends on the claim it is trying to prove, rather than supporting that claim independently.
Background information that helps determine whether evidence supports a claim.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “the conclusion is true” different from “the conclusion is supported by this argument”?
Can background information change whether the same evidence is a good reason?
Is an argument circular whenever its conclusion appears in its premises, or can circularity be more subtle?
Why might an argument transmit support for a conclusion that was already justified?
How could the idea of transmission help explain disagreement about skeptical arguments?
